I literally have high deductible pet insurance with no cap on the dog it makes sense on. And honestly, if you can afford to replace your car, you probably should drop collision. 

And yeah, insurance sometimes pays off, but you’re probably not going to beat the house. Actuaries are good at their jobs. If someone has less than 2K to spend on their dog a year like OP, the appropriate low-deductible insurance policy would eat like a quarter of that budget and/or cap out at like a 5-10k limit anyways. For OP’s budget, “figure out how big a hit you can take, decide if you’ll be okay with putting the dog down if it’s more expensive than that, don’t get a dog if you aren’t” is absolutely the advice I would give, and I work in insurance.

I rescued my dog in 2019 when I was making the same amount. I struggled a lot to pay my bills, take care of her, and get her basic things that dogs of any age need.

I wouldn’t recommend getting a dog until you have better cash flow and savings. I don’t regret getting mine for a second, but I’d be lying to say it wasn’t some of the hardest times of my life. I went without eating more than a few times because her care and needs came first.

Animals are awesome. They’re more expensive than you’d think. On average, I think with food/basic toys/equipment/vet visits that aren’t emergencies, it’s about $2,500 a year. And there’s always emergencies.

While there are ways to reduce costs, I would recommend waiting.

Beyond daily expenses, it’s the emergency bills that you have to keep in mind. Especially as they get older. My dogs (both Pomeranians) only needed their food, supplements, yearly physicals and dental cleanings up to last year, when one of mine got incredibly sick. We’re deep into the 5-figures with his medical care and a lot of those bills came without warning. He suddenly came down with pneumonia and had to be hospitalized for several days. It was around $2000 per DAY to keep him in the hospital and he would have died otherwise. That week, not including the following 2 months of antibiotics and repeated vet checkups, cost about $7000. I didn’t buy pet insurance but I did hold money back in case something like this happened and I’m so glad that I did because it would have absolutely devastated me to have to decline treatment because I couldn’t afford it.

Insurance is very often a lifesaver, literally. Many critical veterinary situations will run you well over $15K, which is way more than you’d pay in insurance. And if you have more than one such issue, you can quickly end up in a situation where you’re making healthcare decisions based on how much debt you can put on a credit card. I agree with your points other than this one, which is so often tossed out there and in my experience it just really isn’t true. (Maybe because we now have so many specialist vets providing cutting-edge treatments to injuries and illnesses.)

Thanks. And yeah, I didn’t mean to be snarky, I just see a lot of people automatically recommending insurance whenever someone is like “finances are a concern”, when you really have to evaluate what you can get and how useful it’ll be.

Honestly, 30k can be enough if you’re careful. I don’t make a ton either, and I’ve had my dog for years. The monthly stuff — food, treats, basic vet — is totally doable on a budget. The real killer is emergencies. One surgery can be $3k-$5k easy. So the trick is: don’t try to save up $5k on your own. Get pet insurance. I pay like $35/month and it covers 80% after a $250 deductible. That’s the only reason I can sleep at night. If you can also put $50/month into a separate savings account just for the dog, even better. 1-2k leftover per year is tight but workable if you have insurance. Without it, you’re one bad day away from a really hard choice. Also, consider adopting an adult dog instead of a puppy. Less chaos, often already trained, and you’ll know more about their health upfront. You clearly care enough to ask this, which already puts you ahead of a lot of people. Go for it, just get the insurance first.

My dad was comatose in the hospital for several days. Since I lived in another state, I stayed at his house and drove his car to visit him at the hospital and come home late. Every time I pulled into the driveway, I could hear his dog whine and get excited, only to be disappointed when I walked in without my dad.

After my dad passed, I wiped his face with a tissue to pick up his scent. When I got home that night, I let his dog sniff the tissue. He took several big sniffs and lay down. After that, he no longer got excited when he heard me drive my dad's car into the driveway.
